feedback: When the right cue keeps the route: 'That cue helped keep the animal on track — this is one real way animals find their way.'

When a cue is mismatched and the route wanders: 'Cues help the animal stay on course — real migrants usually combine several of these cues, so navigation is a real skill, not something they magically know.'
On salmon: 'Salmon can smell their way back to the river where they hatched.'
activities.intendedInsight: Animals do not 'just know' the way — they use real, nameable cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell), often several together, to navigate long journeys.
learnerActions: Take control of a migrant and try to stay on its route, using the animal's real cues: the sun's position, the stars, Earth's magnetic field, coastal landmarks, or (for salmon) the smell of its home river.
Try the cues one at a time as a game, then notice that real animals often use several cues together to stay on course.
Match each cue to an animal that famously uses it (e.g. salmon and home-river smell).
activities.title: Steer by the animal's navigation cues

feedback: If a learner says they should just stay where it's warm: 'If it were only about warmth, they'd never come back. In the northern spring and summer there's a burst of insects to eat and safe places to nest — that's why they return.'
If a learner confuses migration with hibernation: 'Hibernators stay put and sleep through winter; migrators travel. Which is the swallow doing?'
If a learner describes it as a planned holiday: 'Animals don't book a trip — the journey is an inherited instinct triggered by cues such as the days getting shorter.'
activities.intendedInsight: Migration follows food and breeding across the seasons, not just warmth — which is why there is a return leg. It is distinct from hibernation (stay put and sleep) and is an inherited, instinctive pattern triggered by cues like shortening daylight, not a human-like planned choice.
learnerActions: Consider: every autumn swallows fly thousands of miles from Britain to Africa, then fly all the way back in spring — why not just stay in warm Africa all year? Why make the journey twice?
State a reason the swallows come BACK, not just why they leave.
Decide and explain: is a hedgehog that sleeps all winter migrating? Sort several animals into 'migrates' vs 'hibernates'.
Name another animal that migrates and say what it is travelling towards.

Answer a what-if: if there were plenty of insects in Britain all winter, would the swallows still leave? (Discuss both sides: the urge to leave is inherited and triggered by cues like shortening days, so many might still go, but over many generations food availability shapes where and whether a species migrates.)
activities.title: The return-trip puzzle (talk and reason)

feedback: For 'same butterfly does the whole round trip': 'The monarch round trip spans several generations — no single butterfly makes the whole round trip, even though one generation does fly all the way south to Mexico.'

For a one-off move chosen as migration: 'Migration is a regular there-and-back pattern, usually repeated every year with the seasons (salmon make it once in a lifetime, monarchs across generations) — a single move away is not migration.'
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is defined by being regular, seasonal, and a round trip — and learners can apply that definition to tell true migration from one-off movement and to catch common mistakes.
learnerActions: Match each migrant to its route and its driver (food / breeding / escaping a harsh season).
Put the legs of one journey in the correct order by season.
Choose the statement that correctly defines migration and separate it from a one-off wandering move.
Identify the error in statements like 'the same butterfly flies all the way to Mexico and back' or 'only birds migrate'.
activities.title: Check the definition: match, sequence, define
